Skyroot, HEX20, Exolaunch & OhmSpace team up for Vikram-1’s second orbital mission
articles.summary: Hyderabad : An Indian satellite, an Italian-developed engine and German release technology will share a single ride to space, as four companies from three countries join forces on the second orbital flight of Skyroot Aerospace’s Vikram-1 rocket. Hyderabad-based Skyroot Aerospace announced the partnership on Thursday with HEX20, Exolaunch and OhmSpace. Together they cover every stage of the mission, the rocket, the satellite, the system that releases it in orbit, and the engine that will be tested in space. The announcement was made at Space Tech Expo Europe 2026 in Bremen, Germany on Thursday. Hyderabad-based MEIL Group raises $700 million from global investors, firm valued at Rs 1 lakh crore The mission centres on NILA III, the third satellite in HEX20’s NILA series. HEX20 is a small-satellite company based in Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala. The satellite is a CubeSat, a compact spacecraft built from standard 10 cm cubes. NILA III is a “4U” satellite. It will launch alongside Skyroot’s own 4U satellite, SCOPE. Both will travel inside a single 8U deployer, a spring-loaded container that pushes satellites out once the rocket reaches orbit. The deployer is supplied by Exolaunch, a Germany-based company that manages launch missions and handles satellite integration and release. NILA III will also carry a passenger of its own, a high-temperature resistojet built by OhmSpace. A resistojet is a small thruster that heats a gas to produce thrust and can help satellites change or hold their orbit. OhmSpace is an Italian propulsion company with a UK subsidiary that develops electric propulsion for small satellites. The device will be flown as an in-orbit demonstration, a real-world test in space. Two 4U satellites sharing a single 8U deployer is a neat bit of arithmetic, and a practical demonstration of how well-coordinated integration and deployment can make rideshare missions more efficient. None of these partners are meeting for the first time. The mission builds on Skyroot’s launch partnerships with HEX20 and Exolaunch, and on HEX20’s work with OhmSpace on propulsion technology demonstration. As the global small satellite market grows, launch providers, satellite manufacturers, deployment specialists and propulsion developers increasingly need to work as one team. This mission puts companies from India, Germany and Italy on the same flight, showing how specialised capabilities across the space value chain can come together in a single launch opportunity. It also carries a distinctly Indian thread that a spacecraft built by HEX20, launching aboard a Skyroot Aerospace launch vehicle. “Making space more accessible requires strong partnerships across the entire value chain. This mission brings together four companies with complementary capabilities, from launch and satellite development to deployment and propulsion. We are pleased to bring these technologies together aboard Vikram-1 as we expand our international customer and partner ecosystem,” said Pawan Kumar Chandana, Co-founder and CEO of Skyroot Aerospace. Hyderabad-based company Sigma joins hands with Spanish firm to make advanced defence systems in India For Skyroot, the mission reinforces its commitment to opening space for customers and technology partners worldwide through the Vikram series of launch vehicles. For HEX20 and OhmSpace, NILA III is a chance to advance the demonstration of in-space propulsion technology, while Exolaunch’s deployment infrastructure will support the integration and release of both spacecraft. “NILA III was originally scheduled to be launched on SpaceX Transporter through Exolaunch, and moving it to Skyroot Aerospace’s launch vehicle signifies a coming of age moment for the Indian space ecosystem,” said Amal Chandran, Co-founder and CEO of HEX20.

articles.title: Gaza tank raid: Palestinians return to battered camp after Israel breaches truce
articles.summary: Cairo/ Gaza: Palestinians started returning to their battered Gaza camp on Thursday after Israel’s military said it had concluded a tank raid to dismantle a suspected Hamas tunnel, its biggest ground incursion across the ceasefire line since last year's truce. Posting a message to the people of Gaza on Facebook, the military said its forces ended an "activity against Hamas infrastructure" in the area, and that the main north-south Salahudeen road had been reopened for traffic. Palestinian families had fled a day earlier as tanks rolled down the road, the first time since the October 2025 ceasefire that Israeli troops publicly announced a raid deep beyond the boundary line between Israeli and Hamas control. On Thursday, some returned to check their properties in the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza, the focus of the Israeli raid. Israeli military targets Hamas infrastructure in Gaza, kills three 'We are tired' "The entire area has been destroyed, and we honestly do not know what to do,” Abd Aliwa, 44, told Reuters as he sat beside a pile of rubble. "We are tired from all this suffering. We need someone to find a solution for us ... Those who live in tents, they drown. Those who are on the streets, they get wounded. Those who are here, they get wounded." Others stayed away, saying the road was still dangerous and that there was sporadic gunfire. Reuters video showed tank tracks across areas of rubble and open ground, as well as wrecked roads and buildings, though there was no independent confirmation of when that damage took place. On Wednesday, Israel’s military said troops and intelligence personnel had begun “a targeted operational activity” to dismantle what it described as a tunnel west of the yellow ceasefire line that posed a threat to its troops. The military said civilians had been warned to avoid the area. Fearing a renewed military assault, Palestinian families, most of whom have been displaced multiple times since the start of the war in 2023, piled their belongings on top of bicycles, wheelchairs, motorcycles and vehicles as they fled. The Hamas-run Gaza government media office put the number of those who quit the area on Wednesday at around 6,000. 'Can't bear to look at it': Ramadan begins in Gaza amid ruins of shattered mosques 'No truce has come' Mona Shehadeh was among the many who stayed away on Thursday. She said her family fled as the Israeli forces moved in, and moved to a tent originally used as a makeshift school. "We own nothing. Just when we start to establish ourselves, bring in things, stay and settle down, then (another) displacement happens, we leave everything behind," the 37-year-old said. "The war has neither finished nor ended, and no truce has come ... It is all lies," she told Reuters. They had already been displaced about 20 times during the war, she added. Later on Thursday, health officials in the enclave said two Palestinians were killed by Israeli tank shelling in the Zeitoun neighbourhood in eastern Gaza City. The Israeli military did not immediately comment on that report. Israel, which says Hamas has recently been regrouping and rearming, has stepped up attacks against the Islamist group. Hamas has accused Israel of attempting to derail the October 2025 US-brokered ceasefire agreement. UN inquiry says Israel kept committing genocide in Gaza after truce The US-backed body overseeing the truce accused both Israel and Hamas militants of failing to meet their commitments to end hostilities. Nearly all of Gaza's more than 2 million residents are now confined to around a third of the coastal territory, mainly in makeshift tents or damaged buildings under Hamas control. Israeli forces have largely razed and depopulated the two-thirds of Gaza that they still occupy. More than 74,000 people in Gaza have been killed in the military campaign that Israel launched there after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel in an attack on October 7, 2023. Gaza health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli strikes since the ceasefire went into effect, while the Israeli military says 5 Israeli soldiers have been killed.

articles.summary: New Delhi: Justice Yashwant Varma has told Parliament that the impeachment proceedings against him have become "infructuous" and would be "without constitutional foundation" following his resignation, even as he insisted that he is "innocent" of the allegations that included that he possessed "ill-gotten funds", sources said. His response through a letter on September 10 came following the Lok Sabha Secretariat sharing the report of the Judges Inquiry Committee that found him in the wrong, claiming that the charges of discovery of "unexplained" cash at his residence, interfering with evidence and providing evasive explanation on the sequence of events have been "proved". Over 100 Indonesian lawmakers sign petition that could lead to vice president's impeachment The report was tabled in Parliament on August 12. Justice Varma, who was transferred to Allahabad High Court from Delhi High Court after the recovery of a large amount of cash in burnt condition after a fire incident at his official residence here, had resigned on April 9 in the midst of the inquiry. In the two-page letter, which also annexed the resignation letter to the President and another letter to the inquiry panel sent on April 9, he said he has neither drawn salary nor received any facility, allowance, benefit or perquisite attached to the office of a high court judge after his resignation. Citing a 1978 Supreme Court judgement that maintained that a resignation by a judge "takes effect 'ex proprio vigore', that is, by its own force with immediate effect or on and from the date that may be specified" he, said, "thus, upon tendering my resignation in writing with immediate effect, I ceased to hold the office of a Judge on 9 April, 2026 itself, and my entire relationship with the office was severed." "Upon my resignation, proceedings directed towards my removal from office did not survive and cannot be continued. The constitutional power under Articles 124(4), 124(5), and 217 of the Constitution is a power to remove a sitting Judge from office. The said power is not envisaged to be exercised against a former Judge who has ceased to hold office. This position has also been consistently recognised in parliamentary practice," he said. The inquiry report had claimed that Justice Varma had "failed" to provide a "satisfactory explanation" regarding the "presence, source or ownership" of "substantial unexplained Rs 500 denomination currency notes" found in the storeroom in his official residential premises on Tughlaq Crescent in Delhi. In his last letter to the inquiry panel on April 9 withdrawing from the proceedings following his resignation, Justice Varma had denied the charges saying it "defies ordinary logic and common sense" that he chose to store cash in a place which is accessible to several people. He also said the argument that his residence was a secured premise was not correct as the CRPF officer who appeared as a witness had maintained that the back gate to the residence was unmanned and the security was limited to the main entrance. Justice Varma also denied the findings in the report that he gave an “evasive explanation” was not correct and insisted that a “plain reading” of his response on 22 March, 2025 showed no denial of recovery of cash. He also questioned the dropping a number of witnesses from the proceedings.

articles.title: Renewables, electrification help India chase energy independence: IEA
articles.summary: Bengaluru: India energy demand over the next decade surpasses that of than any other country or region in the world but increasing electrification and steps taken to meet its ambition for energy independence by 2047 will help reduce dependency on fossil fuels, says a new assessment by the International Energy Agency (IEA). In its World Energy Outlook released on Thursday, the intergovernmental agency noted that India was set to add 12,000 cars every day over the next decade and see a 33 per cent rise in built spaces, 20 crore air conditioners and increase in production of iron, steel and cement. The report noted that in the current situation where 40 per cent of its energy demand is met by imports, India has struggled to meet its energy needs due to the disruptions in West Asia. However, it acknowledged the "evolving" energy landscape characterised by rising electrification of end uses. World absorbs historic Iran war oil supply loss, but depleted stocks bring risks "This rapid electrification is being accompanied by an increase in the share of low-emissions sources in the generation mix. Solar PV provided half of India’s capacity additions over the past decade, and in 2025, India met its target for half of installed power capacity to be non-fossil five years sooner than planned," it said The analysis said that following the current policies would help India achieve 51 per cent electricity generation from non-fossil sources by 2035. However, the policies also push India's emissions growth, set to be the "largest of all countries". A combination of energy efficiency, electrification and low-emissions will help reduce reliance on imported fuels by adopting additional responses, it noted. Such additional responses include 30 per cent faster adoption of electric cars, acceleration of electrification and energy efficiency, use of renewables and domestic coal in power generation. Such measures will take the country closer to energy independence by 2047. Strait of Hormuz shock: Hidden cost of energy dependence and India's quest for strategic security LPG challenge While India imports most of its oil, its refining sector has grown to the capacity of 6 million barrels/day, surpassing the domestic consumption of 5.7 million barrels/day of oil products. Another 1 million barrel/day capacity to be added in the coming days. However, the growing demand for liquified petroleum gas (LPG) remains a challenge. Even by 2035, India will have a capacity to supply LPG of less than 100 kilo barrels/day compared to the demand of 400 kilo barrels/day. articles.title: Aadhaar card by itself not proof of date of birth: Delhi High Court
articles.summary: New Delhi: The Delhi High Court has held that Aadhaar card is not, by itself, a proof of date of birth. The court was dealing with a petition concerning a dispute between the date of birth of a workman who was allegedly illegally retrenched by her employer in 2017. Delhi High Court seeks ED, SFIO's stand on Tina Ambani's plea to disclose look-out circular In a judgement passed on November 13, Justice Manoj Kumar Ohri stated that the law on Aadhaar only recognises an Aadhaar number as "proof of identity", and as informed in an office memorandum issued by the UIDAI in 2018, the date of birth in the Aadhaar card is recorded based on documents or the self-declaration furnished by the cardholder. While the employer in this case contended that the workman had attained the age of superannuation - i.e., 58 years - based on the May 20, 1959 date of birth in her Aadhaar card, the respondent workman claimed that her date of birth had to be determined on the basis of the Employees' State Insurance Corporation record, which had 1960 as the year of birth. Agreeing with the workman that she was yet to attain the age of superannuation in 2017, the court stated that her Aadhaar card was not supported by any independent document on record, and it was admittedly received by the management merely two months before her services were brought to an end. "The case of the management, thus, rests solely upon Ex. WW1/7 (Aadhaar). However, an Aadhaar card is not, by itself, proof of date of birth," the court held. "The Office Memorandum dated 20.12.2018 issued by UIDAI, which has been placed on record by the workwoman, clarifies the said position. It records that UIDAI enters the date of birth on the basis of the documents or the self-declaration furnished by the card holder. It further records that the Aadhaar Act, 2016 recognises an Aadhaar number as proof of identity, but does not mention that it can be accepted as proof of date of birth," it observed. Delhi High Court gives 3 weeks to Arvind Kejriwal, other Aam Aadmi Party leaders to respond to criminal contempt case The court concluded that since the ESIC record showed her date of birth as May 20, 1960, the management could not later rely on a different date in an Aadhaar card to end her services a year earlier. The court dismissed the management's petition against the labour court's ruling in favour of the workman and ruled that the termination of her services without compliance with the Industrial Disputes Act was rightly held to be illegal.

articles.title: Important step forward for international justice, return of Rohingya: Sheikh Hasina on ICJ ruling
articles.summary: New Delhi: As the UN's top court on Thursday ruled that Myanmar "committed genocide" against the Rohingya group in 2017, former prime minister of Bangladesh Sheikh Hasina described it as "important step forward for international justice". In a statement issued soon after the judgement, Hasina argued that "Bangladesh played a central role in the investigations and in gathering crucial evidence from witnesses and survivors in the refugee camps". "Those efforts have now come to a successful conclusion," she said. The International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Myanmar "committed genocide" against the Rohingya in the northern Rakhine state during the 2017 "clearance operations", in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention. The top UN court also ordered the Southeast Asian nation to allow tens of thousands of people who fled the violence to return home. The case against Myanmar concerning alleged violations of the Genocide Convention was brought by The Gambia in November, 2019. There was no immediate reaction from the Bangladesh government on the ruling. 'Committed genocide': International Court of Justice finds Myanmar guilty, says 'intended to destroy' Rohingya Muslims Bangladesh hosts over one million Rohingya refugees, most of whom fled from Rakhine state during the 2017 military crackdown. Hasina said the judgement was a "proud moment for Bangladesh" and that she remained committed to supporting the cause of international justice. "This is an important step forward for international justice and the return of the Rohingya to their homes in Rakhine State. I call upon all UN Member States to uphold this judgement and ensure that it is respected by Myanmar," she said. Hasina, who fled her country and left for India in August 2024 following a mass student-led uprising that had toppled her government, said she had "welcomed close to one million traumatised Rohingya refugees fleeing Myanmar" during its operations in 2017. articles.title: NASA's Voyager enters interstellar space after signal delay of one whole day
articles.summary: Washington: In the summer of 2027, the Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 spacecraft will each reach a milestone in time. On Sept. 5 and Aug. 20, respectively, they will each have spent 50 years in space. During their journeys, they first explored the planets of the outer solar system, then travelled to the edge of the solar system. Eventually, they passed into the interstellar medium: the space between stars. Although not the first spacecraft ever launched, these are now the two oldest spacecraft still operating. But before the spacecraft hit their semicentennial, Voyager 1 will also reach a milestone in distance. On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 became the first human-built object of any kind to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth. At that point, it travelled about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers), more than four times the distance from the Sun to Pluto. NASA Crew-12 mission | SpaceX launches four astronauts to International Space Station This achievement is remarkable on many levels. This spacecraft, a functioning relic of 1970s technology, has survived well past its expected lifespan. Of course, the spacecraft no longer works as well as it did in its prime. Eight of its original 10 instruments are not operating, and the output from its plutonium-238 power source degrades a little bit each year. Every so often, a lost signal or technical failure puts Voyager 1 in the headlines again. And, within the next decade, scientists may receive the last signal ever from this far-flung object. But, at least for now, both Voyagers continue to send back data that is helping scientists characterise the unknown territory beyond the solar system. As a space history curator responsible for the National Air and Space Museum’s planetary science collection, I’ve studied how space exploration has changed dramatically over the past 50 years. Through it all, the Voyager probes have consistently collected valuable scientific data that has shaped researchers’ understanding of the solar system – and even what lies beyond it. They’ve also helped set public expectations for what a successful mission looks like. Voyager 1’s long saga Voyager 1 launched on Sept. 5, 1977, 16 days after the identical Voyager 2, from NASA’s launch complex in Cape Canaveral, Florida. Voyager 2 launched first, but Voyager 1 quickly overtook it. These spacecraft were big both in size and in ambition. Each is about the size of a small car, with an extended magnetometer boom, carrying instruments that measure magnetic fields, more than 50 feet (15 meters) long. Each probe explored the gas giants Jupiter and Saturn and returned images from these planets that had higher resolutions than anything returned by their predecessors, Pioneer 10 and 11. They imaged the turbulent atmosphere of Jupiter, discovered faint rings around the planet and captured new details of the rings of Saturn and its many moons. Voyager 2 would go on to explore Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989, completing a grand tour of the solar system, that omitted Pluto. Voyager 1 launched after Voyager 2 so it could be set on a course that took it to Saturn’s largest moon, Titan. Seeing Chandrayaan-3 craft development, US experts wanted India to share space technology with them: ISRO Chief On Nov. 12, 1980, Voyager 1 flew within 4,034 miles (6,492 km) of Titan and returned images of the moon that showed a world shrouded in a dense and substantial atmosphere. Now, several decades later, NASA’s Dragonfly mission is slated to take flight in the mid-2030s and investigate Titan’s atmosphere. This trajectory allowed the probe to image several of Saturn’s other moons and even discover a few new ones. But it also sent Voyager 1 on a course that flung it away from the plane of the planets’ orbits. It has been travelling in that direction ever since, crossing several milestones along the way. It crossed the orbit of Pluto in 1989. On Feb. 14, 1990, before powering off its cameras for the last time, it captured a series of 64 images that together became the first “family portrait” of the solar system. There is no clear definition of what it means to leave the solar system. But Voyager 1 has felt less and less of the Sun’s influence as it moves into interstellar space. In December 2004, it crossed the “termination shock”: the outer boundary of the influence of the high-energy particles that make up the solar wind. On Aug. 15, 2012, it left the protection of the Sun’s magnetic field, making it more susceptible to cosmic radiation. As it crossed this boundary, its instruments detected a sparse layer of superheated plasma: charged gas atoms that are so energetic that their electrons are ripped away from their nuclei. Scientists nicknamed this boundary the “Wall of Fire.” The spacecraft continues to travel through interstellar space, recording how the space environment changes as you move farther away from the Sun with data from two of its original instruments. Meanwhile, failing memory, computer glitches, power issues and challenges with an aging propulsion system have led to several nail-biting moments over the past decade in which it seemed scientists might lose contact with the mission forever. Remarkably, NASA engineers have always found a way to use backup thrusters and reroute data to keep the spacecraft operating, long enough to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth. Going the distance So what actually is one light-day? When talking about the distance from the Earth to the Moon, or from the Earth to Mars or Venus, you’d still use miles or kilometers. But once you travel farther than the distance between Earth and its nearest neighbors, the number of miles starts to increase exponentially. NASA delays Artemis 2 moon mission to March due to liquid hydrogen leak Outside of the inner solar system, scientists start to use a larger unit of measure: the astronomical unit (AU), one of which equals the distance between the Sun and Earth. The Kuiper Belt, for example, where Pluto is found, covers a wide swath between 30 and 50 AUs from the Sun. The inner solar system, with Earth and all of the rocky planets, is only an incredibly small fraction of the solar system, and the units of measurement used on Earth don’t really scale well as you move farther away from the planet. Outside of the solar system, scientists start to talk in terms of time: light-years, or, more precisely, the distance light travels in a year. One light-year is equivalent to 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion km), or 63,241.1 AU. The nearest neighboring star to our solar system is Proxima Centauri, which is about 4.25 light-years away. Voyager 1 is now, after 50 years, almost 1 light-day away from Earth. That’s a big distance compared with our usual frame of reference, but it’s still just a fraction of a light-year. While traveling at 37,844.49 mph (60,773 kmh), it will take another 300 years for Voyager 1 to encounter the Oort Cloud that surrounds the solar system, which no one has actually seen, and another 30,000 years to pass through it. From a galactic perspective, after nearly 50 years, Voyager 1 is out the door but has barely entered the front yard. Covering multiple light years and actually making it near a neighbor’s house, like Alpha Centauri, which refers to a system of stars that orbit with Proxima Centauri, would be a 75,000-year trip, if Voyager 1 were headed that way. Until scientists develop technologies to carry people between the stars, like those found in science fiction – if they ever do – people will continue to send increasingly capable robotic spacecraft as our emissaries to help us learn more about the space and worlds beyond our reach. Voyager 1's 'one light day' from Earth: Another milestone in a journey of never turning back Sending a message Maybe, many thousands of years from now, some other space-faring civilization from a distant planetary system will discover Voyager 1. The spacecraft famously carries a gold-plated copper phonograph record that includes greetings, messages, sounds and music, along with encoded images of life on Earth. Many people continue to believe that the exploration of the cosmos can represent the peaceful aspirations of all of humanity. And they continue to want to connect with this great exploratory endeavor by signing their names, literally and culturally, on these great works of technology. We may never hear back from anyone. But we will at least have tried to fill the insurmountable distances of deep space with a bit of ourselves and our culture.

articles.summary: New Delhi: Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Thursday said Kashmir is now free of locally recruited terrorists following the elimination of LeT terrorist Lateef Bhat by security forces. This marks a major milestone in the fight against terrorism, he said at an anti-terror conference here. 'Nation salutes brave jawans': Amit Shah after Lashkar-e-Taiba's terrorist killed in Jammu Kashmir encounter "Under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, we have adopted a 'Zero Tolerance' policy towards terrorism, and this policy is yielding positive results," the Home Minister said. "Following the killing of Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorist Lateef Bhat, Kashmir is now free of locally recruited terrorists born in India. This marks a major milestone in the fight against terrorism," he said. Bhat, who carried a reward of Rs 15 lakh and was wanted for a November 11 attack on a CRPF post that left three paramilitary personnel injured, was neutralised on Wednesday in an encounter in South Kashmir's Kulgam district. To completely eliminate terrorism, organised crime and drug-related problems, Shah said it is essential to bring offenders hiding abroad back to India. Since 2019, 303 fugitives have been brought back to India from 36 countries, he said. "It is essential to dismantle the entire terror financing network. To achieve this, better coordination with agencies responsible for financial investigations is necessary," the Home Minister said. Shah said that India has been a victim of terrorism and "we have been confronting" it "for a long time". He said that police forces of different states had made various efforts, but a lack of coordinated action was clearly visible. "Over time, during the tenures of successive governments, gradual efforts were made to overcome these shortcomings. Today, we can say with satisfaction that in this vast country -- from Kashmir to Kanyakumari and from Dwarka to Kamakhya -- we are putting in place a system under which a uniform strategy to combat terrorism will operate right down to the level of every police station," Shah said. He said the dismantling of the Popular Front of India (PFI), a banned outfit, network is a significant example of how effective coordinated operations by police forces across India can be. In a single night, police forces from 11 states, along with central agencies, jointly dealt a major blow to the PFI network. This operation is now a case study for the entire world, Shah added. Shah on Thursday inaugurated the two-day key anti-terror conference, which will deliberate on "cross-border terrorism" besides the development of future-ready strategies and the strengthening of institutional capacities to meet emerging national security challenges. It is being attended by senior police officers of states and Union Territories, officers of central agencies and departments dealing with counter-terrorism, and experts from allied fields including law, forensics and technology. Held annually, the conference has steadily grown into a significant gathering of operational forces, agencies working in the field of counter-terrorism and experts from the technical, legal and forensic domains. Carpenter, college dropout: LeT commander Lateef Bhat killed in Kulgam encounter, a year after picking up gun It offers agencies/forces an opportunity to collectively examine matters that have bearing on national security and the threats arising from terrorism. The conference sessions will address a range of subjects, including obtaining evidence from foreign jurisdictions, the application of digital forensics and data analysis in counter-terrorism investigations, and the effective management of trials, it said. Sessions will also cover countering radicalisation and emerging hybrid threats to national security.

articles.title: Centre proposes mandatory central clearance for antibiotic manufacturing
articles.summary: New Delhi: With antimicrobial resistance posing a major public health threat, the Union Health Ministry has proposed a mandatory clearance from the central drug licensing authority to manufacture antibiotics apart from approvals from the states, putting an additional layer of scrutiny in place before the medicines hit the market. An amendment has been proposed in the New Drugs and Clinical Trial Rules under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, allowing the Drugs Controller of India to have a new supervisory role for the production of antimicrobials. Centre proposes separate licensing framework for wholesale trade of bulk drugs "The exact requirements for license application at Central Drug Standard Control Organisation will be detailed later. But once the draft rules are notified, the manufacturers will have to get clearance from the Central Licensing Authority as well in addition to the State Drug Authority as an added safety layer for any antimicrobial drug," sources told DH . Antimicrobial resistance is a severe public health crisis in India, which faces one of the highest burdens of infectious diseases and drug resistance globally. According to estimates from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, drug-resistant bacterial infections cause roughly 267,000 deaths and were associated with nearly 987,000 deaths in India in a single year. The proposed amendment, according to the Union Health Ministry, has been initiated in view of concerns regarding the grant of manufacturing licences for antimicrobial products without adequate regulatory scrutiny, including the requirement for studies such as bioavailability/bioequivalence and stability studies. Stability tests are mandatory for the antimicrobials license in most of the states. Sources said the amendment would streamline the process and bring uniformity in grant of licenses. Currently each state has different regulations for grant of licenses. FDA asks weight loss drugs to bear warning against rare eye blindness: Are we too early to trust GLPs? The absence of such assessments may affect the quality, safety and efficacy of antimicrobial products. Substandard or ineffective antimicrobials can contribute to the development and spread of antimicrobial resistance, posing risks to patient safety. Issued on Nov 6, the draft amendment is open to public comments for the next 30 days, following which the government will take a decision on its finalisation.

Gujarat ATS arrests six for stealing 8000 litres of crude oil from ONGC The Congress leader was referring to Amreli district police's investigation into digital investment scam involving "SD Pay" mobile app through which 6.52 lakh people are said to have been duped across the country with majority of the victims from Gujarat. The modus operandi of the scam involved a multi-level marketing network operating through a digital platform. articles.summary: Guwahati: Apanang and Alang - two tiny migratory Amur Falcon birds - which were satellite tagged in Manipur last year, left for their second cycle of their 30,000 km long aerial trip and were tracked flying over the Arabian Sea on Thursday. Three birds were fitted with satellite transmitters on November 11, 2025 and were released at Chiuluan village in Manipur's Tamenglong district, one of their preferred roosting sites in Northeast India. But the third bird, Ahu, did not move from Horn of Africa since November 18, 2025 even as the transmitter was active. Apanang and Alang reached Manipur on October 22, completing their first cycle of migration. After spending 25 days in their roosting sites, the two birds resumed their onward journey on November 17, along with other flocks. "We have set the target of studying their migration route for five consecutive cycles. The main purpose is to study the migration routes and try to extract data and information about possible impact of climate change and other factors on their habitats," Amit Kaler, the Divisional Forest Officer (DFO) of Tamenglong, told DH on Thursday. The two birds were satellite tagged as part of the second phase of a joint project of Wildlife Institute of India, Dehradun and Manipur forest department. Bengaluru’s unique feather library helps identify and study bird species Locally called Akhoipuina in Rongmei Naga dialect in Tamenglong, locals await for arrival of lakhs of tiny Amur falcons (26 to 30cm long and weighing 97 to 195 grams) en route from their breeding grounds in Siberia, Mongolia and North and East China to the warmer south, and finally to South Africa. In October and November, the falcons stops parts of Manipur, Nagaland, Meghalaya and Assam for roosting. In Tamenglong, the birds roost in the bamboo forests along the Barak and Irang rivers and to feed before the longest leg of their journey. Researchers had stated that feasting on the termites emerging in and around the stopover sites, the Amur falcons build up the fat reserves that are critical for the next leg of migration: a six-day non-stop flight of nearly 6,000 km to Somalia, which includes a 3,000 km Arabian Sea crossing. Being warm-blooded, Amur Falcons migrate towards warmer African region during the winter and return to their breeding ground in May. Community involvement Initially, Tamenglong and other roosting sites in the Northeast witnessed largescale hunting of the birds. But constant awareness by the forest department as well as local NGOs and clubs resulted in significant reduction or prevention of hunting. The administration impose ban on hunting, deposit of licenced airguns, beside public awareness to prevent hunting and explore tourism potential during the roosting time. Amur Falcons are protected under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. The Amur Falcons were first satellite tagged in Tamenglong in 2018. The same was done in 2020, 2022, 2024 and 2025.

articles.title: SC custody order: German mother may relocate four-year-old son to Singapore
articles.summary: New Delhi: The Supreme Court on Thursday granted interim custody of a four-year-old boy to his unmarried German mother and permitted her to relocate him to Singapore for schooling, subject to strict safeguards including a Singapore court mirror order and a Rs one crore deposit. A bench of Justices N Kotiswar Singh and N V Anjaria ruled that the pendency of guardianship proceedings does not make a habeas corpus plea for interim custody infructuous. Supreme Court to hear marital rape pleas for final hearing in December In exercise of its parens patriae jurisdiction, the court prioritised the child’s welfare. “In this proceeding, we are seeking to protect the autonomy of a child and help preserve his magical world which unfortunately appears to be seriously jeopardised by the bitter bickering between the parents,” the bench said. The mother, a German citizen working as Vice President of Public Policy at a major international firm in Singapore, and the Indian father, a Delhi-based lawyer, are unmarried. Their son, born in New Delhi on July 15, 2022, holds a German passport. He had lived mainly in Delhi and Goa with both parents before their relationship broke down. The mother approached the Bombay High Court’s Goa Bench in February 2026 alleging denial of access. After the High Court adjourned the matter, she moved the Supreme Court. NIMHANS assessments found both parents capable but flagged their conflict as the key risk to the child. Rejecting the father’s jurisdictional challenge, the bench held, “Irrespective of the nature of the proceeding before a court, when the custody right over a child is involved, the child’s best interests must be the preeminent consideration; it must prevail over all other considerations.” It added that once the child’s welfare is central, “all other interests and considerations must be subservient to it… Even international jurisdictional issues cannot come in the way of the best interests of the child.” The court noted the parents’ “entrenched differences have left the child’s welfare caught in the vortex of their discord.” Applying the triple test of interim relief, it found the mother had a better prima facie claim. “In the case of a child born to unwed parents, the mother has a better prima facie claim of custody,” the court said, also finding the four-year-old was “too young to be able to express an opinion.” Balance of convenience and risk of irreparable harm also favoured the mother, given her employment and concrete schooling plan at UWCSEA or a similar institution. The court stressed that custody orders are temporary. “What is in the best interests of a child who is four years old will not be the same once the child is ten or fifteen years old,” the bench said as it transferred the High Court petition to itself under Article 142. As per the directions, the mother must secure a Singapore mirror order within three weeks and deposit one crore. The father gets daily video access of at least 20 minutes and physical visits. The child must spend longer school holidays in India. Six-monthly psychological assessments were also ordered. Compliance is listed for December 7. The Family Court will decide permanent guardianship independently.

Common antibiotics failing against typhoid, UTI, diarrhoea, skin & blood infections: ICMR
articles.summary: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global public health concern, and its effect is evident in common antibiotics failing to show effective results in treating common infections like typhoid, diarrhoea, urinary tract infection (UTI), and skin and blood infections, according to a recently released Indian Council of Medical Research’s (ICMR) AMR report 2025. The annual report card has shown that bacteria and fungi have learned how to survive the antibiotics meant to kill them. Researchers across 64 hospitals tested over 1.33 lakh patient samples in 2025 to study which germs are spreading and which medicines still work.​ Escherichia coli , the most common cause of urinary tract infections, no longer responds well to common everyday antibiotics like ciprofloxacin or standard cephalosporin tablets. Another key finding is that common fluoroquinolone antibiotics (like ciprofloxacin and ofloxacin) have become almost useless against typhoid and bacterial diarrhoea in India.​ More than half of Staphylococcus aureus skin and blood infections in major hospitals are found resistant to standard penicillin-type drugs. In large hospitals and ICUs, germs like Klebsiella pneumoniae and Acinetobacter baumannii have developed resistance even to carbapenems, which are "last resort" antibiotics reserved for severe or multidrug-resistant bacterial infections.The ICMR report stated that over 90 per cent of Acinetobacter samples in big hospitals resisted these last-resort drugs.​ These findings are crucial because antibiotics are one of the most important discoveries in the healthcare sector. They have saved the lives of millions of people. Over the years, their indiscriminate use has caused people to develop resistance to these drugs. The issue is severe in hospitals with 500 beds or more, where Acinetobacter responsiveness to carbapenems drugs has dropped to 16 to 21 per cent, implying that these medicines do not work four out of five times. Therefore, researchers recommend that hospitals regularly track such trends in the future and rely on laboratory tests for selecting targeted treatments. More importantly, people need be educated to stop overusing antibiotics to further worsen resistance towards them.

articles.title: Google is disrupting itself with its embrace of artificial intelligence
articles.summary: San Francisco: Marshall Evans, a marketer who works with small businesses, has helped home repair companies, fitness studios and other mom-and-pop companies buy Google search ads for more than a decade. The ads — which are tailored to show up when people search on Google for a related term — have been effective in helping a business appear at the top of search results, increasing the chances that someone will click on the ad. Best of 2026: Top Android gaming titles on Google Play Store in India But now those traditional search ads often appear much lower, as Google highlights artificial intelligence-written responses to user queries above its usual list of links and ads. “AI takes over such a large amount of the search results now,” Evans said. Evans’ experience is an example of how AI has disrupted Google’s core business of search advertising. As the company plows hundreds of billions of dollars into developing AI and incorporating the technology across its services, some longtime advertisers are having second thoughts. Over the past six months, Evans, who is based in North Carolina, has moved ad dollars away from Google search ads. For one company that sells trophies, he said, he is allocating $500 a month to the search ads, down from $2,000 a month about a year ago, when Google introduced a feature called AI Mode. And he is putting more of the money toward streaming services such as Tubi, other search engines like Bing and social media sites like Reddit and Nextdoor. Last month, Google reported for the first time that search advertising had fallen to less than 50 per cent of its $128 billion in quarterly revenue. Search ad revenue rose 12 per cent, falling short of the 15 per cent that Wall Street expected. In effect, AI has become a double-edged sword for even the biggest companies. While Google stands to benefit enormously from the technology, including in its booming cloud computing business, AI is also taking a toll as the behemoth adjusts to the technology’s effects. “Google is trying to take a business that was the best business in the world for 10 years and transform it into a different business that doesn’t have the same advantages,” Thomas Monteiro, a senior analyst at Investing.com, said of the move from search to AI ads. “Making that transition is a lot harder than Google’s management thought it would be.” Google’s executives have said the company wanted to make AI search features appealing to users and would think about advertising later. At the top of its search results page, users often now see AI Overviews, an AI-written answer to the user’s query. The bottom of the summary also invites users to interact with a chatbot through the AI Mode feature. Advertising in its AI answers and chatbots has not yet taken off. “We are focused on building the best search user experience, followed by monetization,” Google CEO Sundar Pichai said during the earnings call. Google said that users were flocking to its AI search tools and that the number of search queries was growing faster than it had in the past five years. “AI is driving an expansionary moment for Search, with our AI features leading to increased usage and overall query growth, including commercial queries,” said Thomas Schoenfelder, a Google spokesperson. “Our ads experiments have shown promising results, and we’re confident about our trajectory.” Advertisers can pay more for the chance to feature their ads in AI Mode, but there is no guarantee that the promotion will show up. When ads appear in AI results, some advertisers say, people are getting caught up in back-and-forth discussions with chatbots instead of clicking their ad and visiting their websites. “What we’re seeing is arguably the biggest change in searcher behavior,” said Valerie Schlosser, a marketing executive at VML, a global creative agency in New York. Whether people are talking to Google’s chatbot or other chatbots, she said, they are spending more time in conversation and less time surfing the web. Advertisers aren’t abandoning Google search, she added, but are trying to figure out how to survive in the new system. “Clients are very interested, and they want to test new things,” Schlosser said. “They are interested in ChatGPT and Perplexity, but they are also not totally pulling back from Google.” Max Anderson, CEO of OnlyFinder, a service that helps users find creators on adult entertainment site OnlyFans, said Google search ads had become more expensive in recent years. He has been running search ads for OnlyFinder on Google since 2022 and ran ads there for his previous company, a software startup, starting in 2014. “Our ads won’t show on the page at all, or it will show down the page, below an AI Overview,” he said. “Our costs have probably tripled or quadrupled in the last three years.” Apple iCloud+ subscribers to get more perks, including higher gen AI usage soon The solution was to spend less, he said, adding that he was “gradually and mathematically” pulling back as costs rise and was now devoting about half as much spending to Google ads as he did in the early days of the business. Anderson declined to discuss specific spending, saying the numbers were proprietary. Anderson isn’t planning to abandon Google but is flummoxed by how to get his business mentioned in AI Overviews. Google doesn’t offer advertisers a way to buy guaranteed placement in AI Overviews. “We’d love to have a way as a business to predictably play there, but we have not seen one yet,” Anderson said.

articles.title: Indian national Nikhil Gupta to be sentenced on Friday in murder-for-hire plot
articles.summary: New York: Indian national Nikhil Gupta , accused of being involved in a murder-for-hire plot against a Sikh extremist on American soil, will be sentenced here on Friday by a federal judge, with prosecutors seeking a 24-year prison term for him. Gupta, 55, had pleaded guilty earlier this year to charges of murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering, in connection with his efforts to murder Khalistani separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York. Pannun holds dual American and Canadian citizenship. Gupta will be sentenced on November 20 at around 10 am local time by US District Judge Victor Marrero in the Southern District of New York. Pannun murder conspiracy case: US court orders delivery of summonses to Ajit Doval, former RAW chief through Delhi courts Last week, the US government submitted in court that it is seeking a 24-year prison term for Gupta, whose “conduct was as brutal as it was brazen. “He was a crucial participant in a foreign plot to execute a US citizen on US soil. The Court should impose a sentence that reflects the magnitude of the crime and sends a message that the violent silencing of voices in this country will not be tolerated. For these reasons, and all the reasons set forth above, the Government respectfully requests that the Court impose a sentence of 293 months’ imprisonment,” US Attorney James McDonald said in a 20-page submission to Marrero. The government said that Gupta and his co-conspirators, “including at least one Indian Government employee”, plotted to kill an American citizen on US soil because of the “victim’s political ideology". “It is a crime of the utmost seriousness and demands an equally serious penalty…. the Government submits that a sentence at the top of the United States Sentencing Guidelines range of 235 to 293 months’ incarceration is necessary to serve the legitimate purposes of sentencing.” In his sentencing memorandum, Gupta asked that the Court impose a much reduced sentence. Gupta’s lawyers have argued that the Probation Department calculated an advisory Guidelines range of “235 to 293” months imprisonment and has “recommended a substantial downward variance from that range to 144 months imprisonment followed by three years of supervised release. We join in Probation’s request for a significant downward variance from the Guidelines.” Gupta’s lawyers have said that the probation’s recommendation reflects a considered judgment by the officer who interviewed Gupta, reviewed the full investigative record, and weighed the statutory factors. “It takes into account that Gupta has no criminal history of any kind, that he was suffering from untreated alcohol dependence at the time of the offence, and that any lengthy sentence for a fifty-five-year-old man is significant,” his attorneys said, adding that Gupta “does not minimise” the seriousness of what he did. “He agreed to arrange the murder of another person, and that conduct warrants a term of imprisonment. But the sentence this Court imposes should be sufficient, and not greater than necessary, to serve the purposes of sentencing as to this defendant,” Gupta’s lawyers said. In a letter to the court, Gupta said he wishes he could “turn back time to 2023 and undo my mistakes,” and that when he looks back, “I don’t even recognise the man I had become.” In the letter, Gupta describes how, in early 2023, he became distant from his family and began drinking heavily almost every night. Of his family and the people around him, he wrote: “I deeply regretted the suffering I caused them and the people around me.” US prosecutors seeks over 24-year jail term for Nikhil Gupta in Pannun plot He has told the Court that he is “so thankful that my actions did not result in the loss of human life or injury,” which “would have been the greatest regret of my life.” According to the allegations contained in the indictment, other public court documents, and statements made in court, in about 2023, Gupta worked together with others in India and elsewhere, including with co-defendant Vikash Yadav, to plot Pannun’s assassination on US soil. At Yadav’s direction, Gupta contacted an individual whom he believed to be a criminal associate, but who was in fact a confidential source working with the Drug Enforcement Administration for assistance in contracting a hitman to murder Pannun in New York City. Yadav subsequently agreed, in dealings brokered by Gupta, to pay the undercover officer USD 100,000 to murder the Victim. On or about June 9, 2023, Yadav and Gupta arranged for an associate to deliver USD 15,000 in cash to the undercover officer as an advance payment for the murder.

articles.title: Karnataka HC relief for student whose marks card was withheld over phone during scrapped NEET
articles.summary: Bengaluru: The High Court of Karnataka has directed the National Testing Agency (NTA) to issue a marks card to a meritorious student from Ranebennur, which it had withheld for carrying a mobile phone into the exam hall during NEET held on May 3, which was later scrapped. A division bench of Justices M Nagaprasanna and Hema Kulkarni observed that the doors of medical education must undoubtedly remain guarded against unfair means and undeserving claims, but those very doors cannot be slammed upon genuine merit without compelling justification founded in law. NEET-UG candidate caught using mobile phone during re-test, sent to judicial custody Anushka Basavaraj Maidur, a resident of Ranibennur in Haveri district, had appeared for the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (Undergraduate) – NEET (UG), 2026, held on May 3. As the first entrance test was cancelled following allegations of question paper leak, a re-exam was scheduled for June 21, and the petitioner was issued an admit card. However, three days before the re-exam, Anushka was issued a show cause notice, alleging that she had carried a phone into the exam hall on May 3. She approached the high court after the authorities did not issue her the marks card, contending that she had secured high marks, earned a seat purely on merit at the Belagavi Institute of Medical Sciences. Withholding the result itself is a unilateral and ex parte exercise, she argued. On the other hand, the NTA and Medical Counseling Committee submitted that prohibition against carrying a phone into the exam premises is categorical. The division bench observed that a cancelled exam may remain a matter of history and cannot, without sufficient legal justification, be permitted to become a perpetual impediment to a student's future. "Merit is not a matter of charity. It is the reward of perseverance, discipline, dedication and relentless pursuit of excellence. More so, in a competitive examination for admission to a medical course, where lakhs of aspiring students compete for a handful of coveted seats, merit assumes significance far beyond mere numerical achievement," the bench said. It further said: "A meritorious student carries not merely the marks secured in an examination, but the toil of countless sleepless nights, the sacrifices of formative years and the cherished aspiration of entering the noble profession of medicine. To deny such a student the fruits of demonstrated merit on the altar of procedural technicalities or inconsequential trivialities would be to permit form to triumph over substance and arbitrariness to eclipse excellence,” the bench said, while quashing the show-cause notice and sustaining the seat secured by the petitioner at Belagavi.

articles.summary: Bengaluru: From the unification of Karnataka and landmark political developments to farmers’ agitations, literary movements and milestones in Kannada cinema, the history of the State unfolds through newspaper pages and photographs at ‘Kannada-Kannadi’, an archival exhibition organised by Deccan Herald and Prajavani as part of Karnataka Rajyotsava celebrations. Inaugurated on Thursday, the exhibition, being held at Vismaya Gallery, Rangoli Art Center, at MG Road Metro Station, brings together archival material from the two publications, offering visitors a glimpse into Karnataka’s journey through the decades. Karunadotsava | ‘Kannada-Kannadi’ exhibition from Nov 19 to showcase Karnataka’s 70-year journey The exhibition features material from Deccan Herald’s archives dating from November 1, 1956, to May 22, 2025 and Prajavani’s archives from October 10, 1955 to May 22, 2025. Through newspaper reports, photographs and historical coverage, it documents the political, social, cultural and economic developments that shaped the State and its people. Filmmaker Girish Kasaravalli, who visited the exhibition, said the two newspapers had played a significant role in shaping and documenting Karnataka’s history. "Prajavani and Deccan Herald have played a major role in shaping the history of Karnataka. If you glance at this display, you get a glimpse of what has happened in the past. It is an exhibition that takes you through the major milestones of Karnataka," he said. He recalled that, during his childhood, news often took several days to reach remote parts of the State, making the archival journey from 1956 onwards particularly fascinating. Emphasising the importance of historical awareness among younger generations, Kasaravalli said people needed to understand the past to make sense of the present and the future. "Knowing history and the various movements is very important for any person. Otherwise, they will be living in a vacuum. They have to be connected to the past and the present, and this exhibition is a great way to do that," he said. Veteran Kannada writer Hampana described the exhibition as a panoramic vision of Karnataka, bringing together the State’s political, social and cultural milestones. Recalling the occasion when Rashtrakavi Kuvempu was conferred the first Karnataka Ratna award, followed two days later by the honour being bestowed on actor Dr Rajkumar, he said the archival pages brought back memories of two towering personalities. "Karnataka has a rich history of honouring a great actor alongside a great poet. Bringing together all these facets, this exhibition is truly a grand Vishwaroopa Darshana of Karnataka," he said. Hampana congratulated the organisers, particularly TPML Director Sowbhagyalakshmi K T, for conceptualising and putting together the exhibition. He also underlined the contribution of the Deccan Herald and Prajavani group in nurturing a reading culture and taking journalism to every corner of Karnataka. The displays include coverage of the Karnataka unification movement, the Cauvery agitation, farmers’ protests, political developments, literary movements and milestones in Kannada cinema. Visitors can also revisit reports and photographs documenting personalities and events that have gradually faded from public memory. The exhibition is open to visitors from November 20 to 28, between 10 am and 8 pm, at Vismaya Gallery, Rangoli Art Center, MG Road Metro Station.

articles.summary: Actor Sonakshi Sinha has reacted to the heated controversy stirred up by Rahul Gandhi's lap remark while he was recollecting a memory of his parents, Sonia Gandhi and former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi's loving relationship. Sinha weighed in on the controversy via her Instagram Story, slamming critics who blasted Rahul's remark. articles.summary: Bengaluru: Amid protests by the 'dominant' Veerashaiva-Lingayat community, the Cabinet decided Thursday to confiscate copies of Ravi Hanj's book 'Basava Mantapa' and initiate legal action against him and senior journalist Vishweshwar Bhat who published it. "Copies of the book will be seized and a first information report (FIR) will be registered," Deputy Chief Minister G Parameshwara said, briefing reporters after the Cabinet meeting. This came after Veerashaiva-Lingayat leaders across political parties demanded a ban on the book and criminal action against Hanj whom they accused of insulting 12th century reformer Basavanna. The last book that was banned in Karnataka was Valmiki Yaaru? by scholar KS Narayanacharya after protests in the Legislative Council over alleged insults to the Beda (Nayaka/Valmiki) community in 2014. 'Insults Basavanna’s ideas': Lingayat leaders from Congress, BJP demand ban on ‘controversial’ book 'Basava Mantapa' argues that Veerashaivas and Lingayats are the same. This contradicts claims that Lingayatism is an independent religion founded by Basavanna. The bigger controversy, however, erupted after Hanj made ‘objectionable’ remarks about Basavanna during an interview. He later tendered an apology. Parameshwara said the Cabinet decision was based on a petition by Basava Samiti signed by ministers MB Patil, Eshwar Khandre, Basavaraj Rayareddi and other community leaders. Earlier in the day, BJP veteran BS Yediyurappa and party president BY Vijayendra also condemned the book and Hanj's remarks. Addressing a news conference, MB Patil claimed there was a conspiracy behind the attempts to insult Basavanna and the Sharana tradition. “If anyone interferes in our religion, we will no longer remain silent,” he said. He also slammed Bhat for helping bring out the book. Basava Samiti president Aravind Jatti said the book insulted Basavanna’s ideas. “What’s happening now is an ideological conspiracy to undermine the Sharanas' philosophy and Lingayat identity. We know who is behind this,” he said. Meanwhile, Bidari, who attended the book’s launch, announced on social media that the Mahasabha had decided to initiate a criminal case against Hanj “for giving irresponsible, false and derogatory” statements. During the day, a delegation led by Aland Congress legislator BR Patil lodged a police complaint against Hanj.

From booth-level manager to ‘giant slayer’: How V S Babu toppled M K Stalin in Kolathur
articles.summary: Chennai: A veteran North Chennai politician known for working quietly at the grassroots, V S Babu became a ‘giant slayer’ when he unseated the then Tamil Nadu Chief Minister M K Stalin in Kolathur in April 2026. His death has left the high-profile Kolathur seat vacant, taking to six the number of Assembly constituencies in the state set for by-elections. Stalin shares satirical graphic alleging Tamil Nadu turning into 'Vice City' under TVK rule The other five are Tiruchirappalli East, vacated by Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay after he retained Perambur, and Perundurai, Ambasamudram, Viralimalai and Karur. The sitting MLAs of the last four, S Jayakumar, E Subaya, C Vijayabaskar and M R Vijayabhaskar, all of the AIADMK, resigned and joined the ruling TVK. Two other AIADMK MLAs, Maragatham Kumaravel (Madurantakam) and P Sathyabama (Dharapuram), resigned and joined the TVK shortly after the results were declared in May. They were re-elected in October on the party’s Whistle symbol. Babu, a low-profile grassroots organiser, turned giant slayer when he defeated Stalin, polling 82,997 votes to Stalin’s 74,202 and winning by 8,795 votes. The result breached a 15-year DMK fortress, as Stalin had won Kolathur in 2011, 2016 and 2021. Babu had managed Stalin’s maiden campaign in Kolathur in 2011 before being sidelined by the DMK. He joined the Vijay-led Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) in February 2026 and became its candidate. Born V Sundarampillai Babu (1951-2026) and popularly known in political circles as Purasai Babu, he had been with the AIADMK for ten years from 2016. Before that, he was with the DMK, which he joined as an area secretary and rose to become its North Chennai district secretary. He represented the DMK in the Purasawalkam Assembly constituency from 2006 to 2011. He completed his schooling at Singarapillai Higher Secondary School in Villivakkam and lived in Sembiyam, Perambur. No formal invite was received for Sonia Gandhi's book launch in Delhi, says DMK chief Stalin Known across North Chennai, from Ayanavaram and ICF to Purasawalkam and Jamalia, he built his reputation as an organisational strategist and booth-level campaign manager. Babu (75) died at 2.24 pm at a corporate hospital in Aminjikarai, where he had been in the intensive care unit since September 9 with severe respiratory complications, the hospital said. His condition deteriorated after 71 days of intensive care.

articles.title: Employees' Provident Fund Organisation cuts minimum PF balance requirement to 10% from 25%
articles.summary: New Delhi: The Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation ( EPFO ) on Thursday approved a proposal to reduce the minimum balance that must remain in PF accounts from 25 per cent to 10 per cent, a move that would give greater flexibility to subscribers in accessing their retirement savings. EPFO extends ECR filing due date to October 31 Under the existing framework, an EPFO member of upto 55 years of age, are required to retain at least 25 per cent of their eligible provident fund balance when making partial withdrawals. Once the new framework is notified, subscribers would be able to withdraw up to 90 per cent of their eligible PF balance. Sandeep Sehgal, Partner-Tax & Valuations, AKM Global, said the move would give employees more flexibility to manage their finances e.g. meet urgent expenses without resorting to high-cost borrowing. “However, the trade-off seems to be that every rupee withdrawn today also gives up compounding benefits for the interest it could have earned until retirement,” Sehgal added. The EPFO’s Central Board of Trustees, chaired by Union Minister for Labour & Employment Mansukh Mandaviya, also approved a proposal to reduce waiting period requirement PF balance withdrawal in case of unemployment to 2 months from 12 months. Now a person will be able to withdraw PF balance after 2 months of job loss, this will provide greater flexibility in using their retirement savings during financial emergencies or for major expenses. This is the reversal of the old arrangement. The 12 month waiting period was introduced in October 2025. Now it has gone back to the two-month system. Another significant change approved by the EPFO board includes introduction of Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP) for EPF members. It will allow retiring employees to receive their PF savings in regular instalments instead of taking the entire amount in one go. “This reform will enable retiring members to withdraw their accumulated provident fund savings at regular intervals, such as monthly, quarterly or half-yearly, based on their preference,” as per a statement released by the Ministry of Labour & Employment. This facility would provide members with a structured source of periodic income while allowing the remaining corpus to continue generating returns, thereby helping augment their retirement income and supplement their pension benefits. “The facility would be entirely voluntary, with no compulsion on members to opt for withdrawals,” the ministry said. The EPFO’s central board also gave in-principle approval to allow investment of up to 3 per cent of fresh accretion in eligible Alternative Investment Funds. EPFO wage ceiling raised to Rs 25,000 to cover 51 lakh more workers “By proceeding initially through government-backed entities, within the existing investment ceiling and with prescribed safeguards and oversight, EPFO is diversifying its portfolio without compromising on prudence,” said Shrikant Goyal, Managing Director, Getfive Funds. Globally, long-term capital pools such as endowment funds have broadened their portfolios beyond traditional investments into private equity, venture capital and other alternative assets, and this move reflects a similar principle. “It signals growing confidence in AIFs as an asset class and can channel capital into India’s growth story,” Goyal said.

articles.summary: India has nearly 1.4 billion people. And according to the World Bank's latest estimates, just 2.6% of them live in extreme poverty. Nearly 500 million peopple are estimated to have escaped extreme poverty in just around 15 years.. The government can certainly claim this as an achievement. And for a government that has made development its biggest political pitch, these numbers make for a compelling story. But does this mean that 97.4% of Indians are doing well economically? Not quite. As I keep saying, the story most times lies beyond the headline, which is why there is another picture of India's economy that deserves attention. Using the government's own consumption survey data, the Thali Index shows that nearly 30% of Indians still struggle to afford two basic, balanced meals a day. RBI reports show household debt is climbing while net financial savings have dropped. And official PLFS data show that, once adjusted for inflation, real wages have barely moved. So how do we reconcile these seemingly contradictory pictures? What exactly does the World Bank's poverty estimate tell us, and what does it leave out? We often come across so many numbers about how much the country is progressing. But how often do we stop to ask what these numbers actually mean? How are they calculated? And what might they be leaving out? At Let Me Explain, we've always tried to break down the data and put them in context. It is important to celebrate India’s achievements but if they are not based on hard realities, then it will help only the government, not the people of the country. We'll keep doing this work. But there are four things we need to look at before accepting this number at face value: How free government benefits are counted. How India's poverty surveys have changed. What's happening to jobs and wages. And whether the poverty line itself is an adequate measure of economic security. Let's start with how India counts its poor. India doesn't measure poverty by asking people how much they earn. Nearly 90% of the workforce is informal, like street vendors, farm workers, construction labourers, with no regular payslips or income records. So instead, government surveys looked at how much households spend. But in the newer consumption surveys of 2022–23 and 2023–24, there's an important change. Surveyors no longer just record what families buy with their own money. They also calculate the value of goods people receive through welfare schemes. Either for free or at subsidised rates. This includes foodgrains through ration shops and other government-provided goods like cooking gas, laptops, cycles, books, uniforms etc. Their estimated market value is added to a household's consumption expenditure. And just like that, the spreadsheet can say a family is no longer poor. Of course, free rations make a real difference. They help families survive. But there's a difference between being able to afford your necessities and depending on government support to meet them. If your escape from poverty depends on subsidies, how financially secure are you? And what happens if those benefits are reduced, or prices rise? There is another problem when we compare poverty figures from 2011 with those from 2023–24. The surveys themselves have changed. In 2011–12, surveyors visited a household once and asked people to recall their expenditure over the previous 30 days. In the newer surveys, households were visited three times, with more detailed questions. Think about your own spending. Can you remember every cup of tea, auto ride or packet of biscuits you bought last month? You probably can't. But if someone asks you several times, with a detailed list of expenses, you're likely to remember more. That means reported household spending can go up simply because of the way questions are asked, not because people are actually spending more. The selection of households and the sampling methods also changed, making direct comparisons with older surveys more complicated. And this isn't just a theoretical concern. When survey methods change this substantially, statisticians normally conduct what's called a bridge survey. They test both methods side by side to understand how much of the difference comes from actual economic improvement and how much comes from the change in methodology. India did not conduct such a survey. Research from the Center for Global Development has pointed out that if India's actual extreme poverty rate is closer to 6% rather than 2.6%, that would mean a difference of around 50 million people. This is a hypothetical difference based on the 6% estimate, There's another striking detail. The World Bank's 2025 estimates put India's extreme poverty rate at 5.3% for 2022–23. The latest brief brings that figure down to 2.6%. So these numbers need to be understood in the context of changing data and methodology. When poverty genuinely falls on a large scale, you would expect to see it reflected in the job market. In the last few years, due to internal and external factors, economic growth has slowed, private investment has stagnated, and factories aren’t creating enough jobs for the millions of young people entering the workforce. Today, more than 45% of India's workforce is still employed in agriculture, even though the sector contributes a much smaller share of the economy. The World Bank's extreme poverty threshold is currently $3 a day, adjusted for purchasing power across countries. But remember, this is a measure of extreme poverty. It is not a measure of whether someone can afford a reasonably secure life. India's own official poverty line hasn't been updated since 2011, when it was pegged at roughly Rs 32 a day. So we are dealing with a poverty benchmark that doesn't adequately reflect today's cost of living. Let's move away from these benchmarks and look at something more tangible: food on a plate. Economists recently used the same 2023–24 government consumption data to calculate something called the Thali Index. The question was simple: Can Indian households afford two basic, balanced meals a day, consisting of staples such as dal, rice, roti and vegetables? Even after accounting for free foodgrains distributed by the government, the findings are stark. Around 40% of rural Indians and 10% of urban Indians cannot afford two basic meals a day. That's nearly 30% of the population. So we have one set of statistics telling us that 97.4% of Indians have escaped extreme poverty, while another suggests that nearly a third cannot afford two balanced meals a day. Now, none of this means India hasn't made progress. Welfare delivery has improved. Basic infrastructure has reached millions of villages. These are real achievements. But a poverty line is essentially a pass-or-fail test. If a school lowers its pass mark to 3 out of 100, suddenly almost everyone may pass. But that doesn't mean the students have learnt more. The benchmark has simply changed. Poverty reduction cannot be measured by one headline number alone. Poverty statistics shape public policy. If the message is that extreme poverty has fallen to just 2.6%, there is a danger that the urgency to address hunger, stagnant wages, unemployment and inequality will disappear. The real question isn't just how many people have crossed an extreme poverty line. It's whether they have the means to live with dignity and financial security. Like LME?
